title: Honor of the humble
hookLine: the Ardas names God by what God is to those with nothing: honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless

cards: Every school has the kid who eats lunch alone. Every office has the person whose name nobody quite remembers. Every family has the cousin who's always in the kitchen while the photos are being taken.
People often reach for big titles when they address God: king, judge, almighty. Near its end, the Ardas also does something quieter.
Just before the one praying turns to their own request, it names God by who God is for exactly those people. The kid at the empty table. The one in the kitchen.

teach.h: MAAN, TAAN, OT: HONOR, STRENGTH, SHELTER.
teach.b: The line runs: nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot, sache pita Waheguru. Honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless, true Father, Waheguru. Look at how it's built.
Maan is honor, dignity, standing. Taan is strength. Ot is shelter, something to lean on.

teach.h: NI-: THE ONES WHO LACK IT.
teach.b: Put ni- in front of each and you get the people who lack it: the nimaana, with no standing; the nitaana, with no strength; the niota, with no one to lean on. So the Ardas doesn't describe God floating far above.
It describes God as the very thing each of them is missing. No honor? God is your honor.
No strength? God is your strength. This isn't new to the prayer.
Guru Nanak said it in his own hymns.

teach.h: GURU NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWLY.
teach.b: In Sri Rag, on ang 15, he says Nanak stands with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to copy the great; and where the lowly are cared for, there the Lord's glance of grace falls. Sikh life tried to make that physical.

teach.h: LANGAR PUTS IT ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: In langar, everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food, whatever their caste or their bank balance.
In the Ardas, the rich donor and the person who came in for a free meal say these words together, standing side by side. So the line works two ways. It's comfort for anyone who feels small today.
And it's a quiet question for anyone who doesn't: if God's honor is with the overlooked, where should mine be?

how: Near the end of the Ardas, Sikhs address God as nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot, the honor, strength and shelter of those without them, just before the specific request of the day.

o: a shelter to lean on in hard times
honor, dignity, a sense of standing

s: this line addresses God with titles like king and judge
it names God as honor, strength and shelter for the people who lack them.
Guru Nanak says he stands with the lowest of the low
Sri Rag, ang 15: he has no wish to copy the great.
in the Ardas, only the poor say this line
the whole congregation says it together, rich and poor side by side.

games.q: you're putting together a prayer meant to be said by everyone, rich and poor. how do you name God just before the request?
o: by the greatest titles you can find.
by what God is to those with nothing.
you skip names and go straight to the request.
games.why: the Ardas calls God the honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless, and only then makes its request.

practice: Bring to mind one person who gets overlooked, at work, at school, maybe in your own family, and see their face.

Notice what they might be missing today, standing, strength, or someone to lean on, and simply hold them in your attention, the way the Ardas holds them. If you pray, say the three words softly: maan, taan, ot.

wordCard.voice: Maan, honor, dignity, standing: the Ardas names God as the honor of those with none, the strength of the weak, the shelter of the shelterless, maan, taan, ot.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: honor, dignity, standing; a nimaana is someone without it.

carryVoice: Your line: strength of the weak. Honor, strength and shelter, for those who have none. That's day six hundred thirty-two.
